why: The structural invariants of a loaded model are checked twice: by the engine in
packages/zig/scene-runner/src/structure.zig, and by the TypeScript host in
packages/ts/scene-runner/src/validate-model.ts. The host's copy is a convenience —
a synchronous ModelValidationError before any engine call — not a second opinion.
Two copies of one rule set is exactly the shape every other shared name in this
repository is gated against: field types, function aliases, the runtime projection,
the model versions, the shared bounds. This one was not. The wording in the two
files is identical, which is what a port looks like, and nothing failed when they
disagreed — the host rejected a valueless binding that a prepare entry fills while
the engine ran it, and no test on either side noticed.
So: `shared` is what both must enforce, and `hostOnly` is what the host adds on
purpose. A rule in neither list, appearing in either file, is drift.
The Go compiler checks the same ground earlier, in internal/validate, and is not
gated here. Its diagnostics carry error codes and source positions and are worded
for an author looking at a .tu file, not for a host handed a model — a different
surface with a different audience, which spec/convert-runtime-spec.md covers.

shared.why: Two scenes with one id make every reference to it ambiguous.
Two routes with one id make dispatch by entryId ambiguous.
entryId resolves against both namespaces, so a shared id is ambiguous.
A route with no entry scene has nowhere to start.
The entry scene must be present before the run begins; unlike a match target, it cannot arrive from an extend hook later.
A transition to a scene that does not exist cannot be taken. Suppressed when the model declares an extend hook, because the target may still arrive.
Two actions with one id make every next rule naming it ambiguous.
A scene whose entry action does not exist cannot start.
The root names the binding whose value is the action's result.
